title: Prepositions and conjunctions

objectives.can: Say which case a preposition takes and what the commonest conjunctions join.
Recognise the commonest prepositions and conjunctions.

explanation.summary: A Latin preposition does not stand alone: it governs a noun in the accusative or the ablative, and the case it demands is part of the word. Conjunctions join words, phrases and clauses. Learning each preposition together with its case turns many short phrases into plain sense.

sections.heading: A preposition governs a case
body: A preposition comes before a noun, pronoun or adjective and sets it in a particular case. Latin has no genitive or dative prepositions of this kind. Every preposition takes the accusative, the ablative, or (in a few cases) both. Learn each one with its case, as you learn a noun with its genitive.

In *per ipsum* the pronoun is accusative, because *per* takes the accusative. In *sine ipso* it is ablative, because *sine* takes the ablative. The preposition and its noun make a prepositional phrase, which usually works like an adverb: it tells where, when, how or why.

sections.heading: Prepositions with the accusative, with the ablative, and with both
body: These lists contain the commonest in the Vulgate and the Fathers.

*in* and *sub* take both cases. With the accusative they show motion toward or into, or purpose: *in tentationem*, 'into temptation'. With the ablative they show where something is: *in cælis*, 'in the heavens'. In the Vulgate *in* with the ablative also sometimes expresses the means or instrument, after the Hebrew.

sections.heading: Reading the case
body: Because the case of the noun is fixed by the preposition, it tells you something about the noun even when the ending is ambiguous. In *de lumine*, the ending -e after *de* can only be ablative. In *ex Deo* the same is true of -o.

Two points need care. *cum* attaches to the personal pronouns of the first and second persons as an ending: *mecum* is *cum me*, 'with me'. And *in* and *sub* change their sense with the case they take; in the text the case of the noun decides. *super* is listed with the accusative, but it can also take the ablative, in the sense 'about'.

A few words are both prepositions and something else. *cum* is a conjunction as well ('when', 'since'): if it is followed by a noun in the ablative, it is a preposition; if it begins a clause with its own verb, it is a conjunction. *post* and *ante* can also be adverbs.

sections.heading: Conjunctions that join
body: *et* is the ordinary word for 'and'. *atque* (also written *adque* or *ac*) is a fuller 'and'. The ending -que is added to the second of two words: *terramque* is 'and the earth'. *sed* means 'but'; *aut* and *vel* mean 'or'.

Some conjunctions never come first. *enim* ('for'), *autem* ('but', 'moreover'), and *igitur* ('therefore') normally stand second in their clause: *Filius autem hominis*, 'but the Son of Man'. This is a useful sign when you look for the start of a clause.

*nam* ('for') opens its clause. The reason or explanation is introduced by *quia* and *quoniam* ('because', 'since'). *si* introduces a condition ('if'). *ut* and *ne* introduce purpose, result and other clauses, which later lessons treat.

misunderstandings: The preposition and the case work together. Do not translate the case ending as well as the preposition: *in cælis* is 'in the heavens', not 'in of the heavens'.
*in* does not always mean 'in'. With the accusative it means 'into' or 'for' or 'against'; with the ablative it means 'in', 'on', 'among' or 'by means of'.
*enim* and *autem* are not the first word of their clause. If you look for them at the start you will not find the clause's beginning.
-que is not part of the word it follows. *deditque* is *dedit* plus -que: 'and he gave'.

deeper.heading: The Hebrew behind the Vulgate's prepositions
body: The Vulgate often translates a Hebrew or Greek preposition by the nearest Latin one even where classical writers would use another construction. Hence *in* with the ablative of means, and *ad* with a person where classical Latin would use the dative. The result is correct Latin of a particular kind, and it is the Latin you will read in this course.

examples.analysis: *per ipsum* is *per* with the accusative: 'through him', the pronoun *ipsum* in the accusative. *sine ipso* is *sine* with the ablative: 'without him', *ipso* in the ablative. Two prepositions in one verse, two cases.

reading.why: The prologue is rich in prepositional phrases (*in principio*, *apud Deum*, *per ipsum*, *sine ipso*, *de lumine*) and in the connectives *et*, *sed* and *ut*, in short sentences.
